9:2.text: And I beheld, and heard an angel flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice, Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth by reason of the other voices of the trumpet of the three angels, which are yet to sound!

provenance.other: “Woe, woe, woe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James Bible doubles a woe twice more (Revelation 18:10, 18:16, both “Alas, alas”) but trebles it only here. “Woe to the inhabiters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 8:13 and 12:12, and the Book of Mormon's “inhabitants” for “inhabiters” is the one word it does not take over.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 24:6 or Revelation 17:2, if the phrase is read as the generic “inhabitants of the earth”, which occurs in exactly seven KJV verses.
provenance.significance: The two Revelation woes are the only two, and this verse has both of them at once. From 8:13 comes the treble woe cried by a flying angel with a loud voice — which is what 9:1 has just described, a voice heard among all the inhabitants of the earth. From 12:12 comes the rest of the sentence: “Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you.” Revelation gives the rejoicing to heaven and the woe to the earth because the devil has been cast down; 3 Nephi 9:2 keeps the woe and the devil and hands the rejoicing to the devil instead — “the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice.” The inversion is the argument. In Revelation the devil's descent is heaven's victory; here it is simply his triumph, and there is nobody left in the heavens to rejoice.

9:2.note: 'Wo, wo, wo unto this people; wo unto the inhabitants of the whole earth, except they shall repent, for the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice.' A threefold woe addressed to the earth's inhabitants, spoken by a voice out of heaven, with the devil named in the following clause: every element is Revelation's, and Revelation uses them in exactly two verses, both of which are here. “rejoice, ye heavens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the devil is come down” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Revelation 12:12; the Book of Mormon keeps the verbs and reassigns them. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not a quotation — the longest continuous run is three words — but the coincidence of a treble woe, the addressees, and the devil in one sentence is not producible from anywhere else in the King James Bible.

9:3.text: Standing afar off for the fear of her torment, saying, Alas, alas that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come.

provenance.other: “that great city” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses. Three are Nineveh (Jonah 1:2, 3:2, 4:11), one is the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:10), and the remaining six are Babylon in Revelation 14:8, 17:18, 18:10, 18:16, 18:19 and 18:21. “utterly burned with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and Revelation 18:8 is the one that burns a city.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:2, on the strength of the same demonstrative and a wickedness that comes up before God; see the separate row at 9:7.
provenance.significance: The demonstrative is doing more work than a reader notices. “That great city” is not how the Book of Mormon otherwise names Nephite cities, and in the King James Bible it is overwhelmingly the epithet of one city under one sentence — the Babylon of Revelation 18, burned with fire in verse 8, cast into the sea like a millstone in verse 21, and found with the blood of prophets and of saints in her at verse 24. 3 Nephi 9 destroys its cities in precisely those three ways and gives that reason: Zarahemla burned with fire (9:3), Moroni sunk in the sea (9:4), and every one of them destroyed so that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up any more (9:5, 9:7, 9:8, 9:9, 9:11). Recover the context and the chapter is reading the whole Nephite civilization as Babylon — which is what makes the survivors' invitation at 9:13 an offer of exile's end rather than merely of forgiveness.

9:3.note: 'Behold, that great city Zarahemla have I burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof.' The formula recurs at 9:4, 9:9 and, without the adjective, throughout 9:6-10; it is adjudicated here at first use. No single Revelation verse is being quoted, and the epithet on its own would not carry a link — ten KJV verses have it. What carries it is that the chapter takes three separate fates from Revelation 18 and distributes them across its cities in Revelation's own order, and closes each with Revelation 18:24's charge. Moderate rather than high because the individual contact is short and the argument is cumulative.
9:3.whyNot: “That great city” is a natural English intensifier and needs no source; Jonah's Nineveh, a great city spared for its repentance, is arguably the more apt model for a chapter that ends by inviting the survivors to repent. The Revelation reading rests on the cluster, not on this phrase.

9:4.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.

provenance.other: “drowned in the depth of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “depth of the sea” in the singular occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Matthew 18:6. The plural “depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10, Micah 7:19) and the Book of Mormon has the plural, so the number is against the link even though the collocation of drowning with the sea's depth is Matthew's alone.
provenance.alternative: Micah 7:19, 'thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea', which supplies the plural but reverses the sense: Micah drowns sins, 3 Nephi 9:4 drowns a city.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:6 is the only verse in the Bible where drowning in the sea's depth is a sentence rather than an accident, and the crime it punishes is offending one of the little ones who believe. Read the chapter to its end and the same figure returns: 'whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive' (9:22). The chapter opens by drowning a city and closes by receiving a child, which is Matthew 18's own sequence — verse 6 sinks the offender, verse 3 sets a child in the midst. Whether the writer saw that or not, the two ends of 3 Nephi 9 sit at the two ends of one Gospel pericope.

9:4.note: 'That great city Moroni have I caused to be sunk in the depths of the sea, and the inhabitants thereof to be drowned.' The verb and the location together are a Matthean singleton. The case is limited by one letter: the Book of Mormon has 'depths', which is the Old Testament's plural, and Matthew has 'depth'. Recorded at moderate because the drowning is what is distinctive — the three plural verses do not drown anybody, they bring people up (Psalm 68:22), dry a way through (Isaiah 51:10), and sink sins (Micah 7:19).
9:4.whyNot: The singular/plural divergence is exactly the kind of one-word test that decides mediation elsewhere in this catalogue, and here it points away from Matthew. A reader who declines the link on that ground is being consistent with the catalogue's own method.

9:5.text: And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth.

provenance.other: “blood of prophets, and of saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The reverse order, “of saints and prophets”, also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:6. Those two are the whole of the King James Bible's usage: nowhere else are prophets and saints named together as the murdered. The Book of Mormon has Revelation 18:24's order, prophets before saints, at all five occurrences of its formula.
provenance.significance: Revelation 18:24 is the verdict clause of Babylon's fall — the sentence that says what the burning was for. 3 Nephi 9 attaches that clause to every city it destroys and turns it into a purpose: not 'in her was found the blood' but 'that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' The blood is still crying; the destruction is what stops the crying. That is a harder theology than Revelation's, because Revelation's Babylon is punished for the blood while 3 Nephi's cities are buried to silence it, and the difference is visible only once the source is recovered.

9:5.note: 'That the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' The pairing is not a natural English collocation; it is Revelation's, and Revelation's twice only, once in each order. The Book of Mormon takes the order of 18:24 — the Babylon verse, not the third-vial verse — and repeats it verbatim at 9:7, 9:8, 9:9 and 9:11, which is why it is adjudicated here at first use. The 1830 reading at this verse is 'shall not come **up** any more', with 'up' deleted in 1920; the first edition therefore has the blood ascending, which is what Genesis 4:10 and Jonah 1:2 both require and what the modern text obscures.

9:7.text: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.

provenance.other: “wickedness is come up before me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the shorter “come up before me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Jonah 1:2. The Book of Mormon does not have the preposition: it has wickedness hidden 'from before my face' and blood that comes 'up any more unto me'. The two halves of Jonah's clause are present, split across the sentence.
provenance.significance: Jonah 1:2 is the King James Bible's one verse in which a city's wickedness comes up before God, and it is also one of the ten verses reading 'that great city' — the epithet 3 Nephi 9 uses of Zarahemla, Moroni, Moronihah and Jacobugath. What makes the recovery worth the effort is Jonah's outcome. Nineveh's wickedness comes up before God and Nineveh is not destroyed; it repents at a prophet's preaching and is spared, and Jonah is angry about it. 3 Nephi 9 runs the same premise to the opposite conclusion, destroys the great cities whose wickedness came up, and then — at 9:13 — offers the survivors exactly what Nineveh got. The chapter is Jonah with the sequence reversed: destruction first, the invitation to repent afterward.

9:7.note: 'And waters have I caused to come up in the stead thereof, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' Two Jonah singletons are in play and neither is reproduced continuously: 'wickedness' + 'come up' + a first-person divine 'me' are all here, distributed across two clauses rather than the one clause Jonah has them in. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion, for that reason.
9:7.whyNot: Split agreement across a clause boundary is exactly what the machine streams cannot see and also what a reader can manufacture at will; 'wickedness' and 'come up' are both common words and the sentence has other business. If the Revelation 18 reading at 9:3 is right, this verse needs no second source.

9:11.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: “crieth unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the shorter “unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Both are Genesis 4:10; blood cries from the ground nowhere else in the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: The chapter has spent nine verses saying that the blood of the prophets must not 'come up any more unto me', and only at 9:11 does it name the mechanism, in Cain's words. That matters for what the destruction is. Genesis 4:10 is God's interrogation of a murderer — 'What hast thou done?' — and the answer to the crying blood there is not the burial of Abel but the marking and exile of Cain. Here the crying blood is answered by burying the murderers with the evidence, which is the one thing Genesis 4 refuses to do. The borrowing carries its own indictment: a reader who recovers the context finds that the God who would not let Cain's ground stay silent is here silencing it himself.

9:11.note: 'That the blood of the prophets and the saints which I sent among them, might not cry unto me from the ground against them.' Four continuous words of a King James singleton, with the fifth — 'cry' for 'crieth' — required by the Book of Mormon's subjunctive. Below any quotation threshold and unmistakable all the same: no other verse in the Bible has blood crying to God out of the earth. The 1830 reads 'which I sent', changed to 'whom' in 1920; the first edition's relative pronoun is the King James Bible's own usage for persons and the modern text has corrected it away from the source.

9:13.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 6:10 — 'and convert, and be healed', with no agent named for the healing.
provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 + Acts 3:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The Isaiah verse and its New Testament forms diverge at exactly two points that this verse reproduces, and the Book of Mormon has the New Testament's reading at both: 'be converted' against Isaiah's active 'convert', and a first-person divine healer against Isaiah's agentless 'be healed'. Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 read 'should be converted'; John 12:40 reads 'and be converted', without the auxiliary, which is what 3 Nephi 9:13 has. The surrounding syntax comes from a second New Testament verse: “and be converted, that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:19, and the Book of Mormon reproduces that four-word sequence with Acts's 'repent' in front of it.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 13:15 or Acts 28:27 for the healing clause, if the missing 'should' is thought too slight to separate the three; all three carry the same two decisive divergences from Isaiah.
provenance.significance: This is the same verse of John that 1 Nephi 12:17 used, and it is used here to undo what it did there. In 1 Nephi the borrowing was from the front half — the blinded eyes and the hardened heart, John's own words and not Isaiah's — as an explanation of why a people would not see. Here the chapter takes the back half, the clause John's Isaiah leaves as a road not taken, and turns it into an offer: be converted, that I may heal you. John 12:40 is a statement about why healing did not happen; 3 Nephi 9:13 addresses the survivors of a destruction with the same clause in the imperative, and the blindness Isaiah's God imposed is the blindness this voice invites them out of. Acts 3:19 supplies the frame, and its own context is worth recovering too: Peter is preaching to the people who have just killed Jesus, promising them 'times of refreshing' if they will repent and be converted. 3 Nephi 9:13 speaks the same offer to another people who have just rejected the same prophets, three days after the same death.

9:13.note: 'Will ye not now return unto me, and repent of your sins, and be converted, that I may heal you?' `mediation-check.py` returns two decisive points against Isaiah 6:10 and for the New Testament form. Isaiah's idiom is intransitive — the people 'convert' and 'are healed', with the healer unnamed — while every New Testament rendering makes the conversion passive and puts the healing in God's own mouth. The Book of Mormon has the passive and the first person, in a first-person divine speech where Isaiah's construction would have served just as well. Two New Testament verses are fused: Acts 3:19 gives the imperative and the syntax — “and be converted, that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon has all four words in order, with 'repent' ahead of them as Acts has it — while John 12:40 gives the completion, since Acts 3:19's own 'that' clause is about sins being blotted out and not about healing. Among the three witnesses to the Isaiah clause, John 12:40 alone drops the auxiliary 'should', which the Book of Mormon also drops.

9:15.text: Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.

provenance.other: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 14:10 and 14:11, and the two are identical across the whole of the shared span, so the pair cannot be separated on wording. John 10:38 has the same doctrine in the reverse order — 'the Father is in me, and I in him' — and is not the source.
provenance.significance: Ten continuous words of the farewell discourse, and the clause that follows them is where the metalepsis is. 'In me hath the Father glorified his name' has no King James phrase behind it, but it has a King James scene: John 12:28, where Jesus prays 'Father, glorify thy name' and 'there came a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again' — a voice the bystanders took for thunder. 3 Nephi 9 is a voice out of darkness heard by a people who have just survived thunder, and the sentence it speaks about the Father's glorified name is the sentence that voice from heaven spoke. The chapter is not only quoting John; it is occupying the one position in John's Gospel from which the Father is heard to speak.

9:15.note: 'I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and in me hath the Father glorified his name.' A ten-word continuous run from a two-verse King James pair, and one of the longest verbatim New Testament runs in the Book of Mormon outside its transcribed blocks. Still short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his long quotations. The speaker's situation is what makes the borrowing pointed: in John these words are spoken to Philip in a room, and here they are spoken out of darkness to a continent.

9:15.text: And when they heard that, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, Lord, thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is:

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 / Acts 4:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “all that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24, and Acts 4:24 is itself an echo of Exodus 20:11. `mediation-check.py` reports no decisive divergence: the two verses do not differ at any point 3 Nephi 9:15 reproduces, so the mediation cannot be settled from this verse and is recorded as uncertain.
provenance.alternative: Nehemiah 9:6, 'the earth, and all things that are therein', which supplies the Book of Mormon's 'things' but not its grammar; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: This is a case where the 1830 first edition preserves the borrowing and every later edition erases it. 'All that in them is' is a King James construction that reads as a solecism in modern English — a singular verb governing a plural antecedent, an artefact of the 1611 translators' Hebrew. The 1830 has 'all things that in them **is**'; 1920 changed 'is' to 'are' and produced a sentence that is grammatical, idiomatic, and no longer in the King James Bible at all. CONVENTIONS §8 was written for exactly this: the first edition shows the dependence and the current text hides it.

9:15.note: 'I created the Heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is.' The King James Bible has this odd concord twice and nowhere else. The Book of Mormon inserts 'things' — probably under the pull of Nehemiah 9:6's 'all things that are therein' — but keeps the singular verb, which only the Exodus/Acts idiom explains. Moderate rather than high because the interpolated word breaks the run, and because the underlying creation formula is common property.

9:15.text: The same was in the beginning with God.

provenance.other: “in the beginning with God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the Word was with God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are the prologue of John. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'the Father' for 'God' throughout, which is the adjustment a first-person speaker requires.
provenance.significance: Verses 15 to 17 of this chapter run down John's prologue in John's order and nothing else's: creation of all things (John 1:3), pre-existence with God (1:2), coming to his own and being rejected (1:11), and the giving of sonship to those who received him (1:12). That the sequence holds across three consecutive Book of Mormon verses is stronger evidence than any one of the four contacts, and it is the reason this row sits at high on a phrase that is only four words long.

9:15.note: 'I was with the Father from the beginning.' The prologue's second verse in the first person, with 'the Father' for 'God'. Taken alone it would be an echo at best; taken as the second step of a four-step walk through John 1:1-12 that continues into 9:16 and 9:17, it is part of an extended borrowing and is graded accordingly.

9:16.text: He came unto his own, and his own received him not.

provenance.other: “his own received him not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The whole of John 1:11 is nine words long and 3 Nephi 9:16 reproduces all nine, changed only from the third person to the first.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon splits this verse across thirty-four years and two speakers. At 3 Nephi 1:14, on the eve of the birth, the voice says only the first half — 'Behold, I come unto my own' — and stops before the rejection. Here, after the crucifixion and the destruction, the same voice finishes the sentence: 'and my own received me not.' The half-quotation at 1:14 is not an abbreviation; it is a sentence held open for three decades, and the reader who knows John's verse knows from 1:14 how it must end.

9:16.note: 'I came unto my own, and my own received me not.' John 1:11 entire, in the first person. The argument for the first-person adaptation was made at 3 Nephi 1:14, where the opening clause appears alone; what is new here is the second clause, which the earlier verse deliberately withheld. This is the completion of a quotation rather than the recurrence of a formula, so it is written as a full link under ADJUDICATING §4.

9:17.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: “become the sons of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “believe on his name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are John 1:12, which is the only verse in the King James Bible joining reception of Christ, sonship, and belief in the name.
provenance.significance: The one substantive change is a deletion, and it changes the doctrine. John gives the received 'power to become the sons of God' — ἐξουσία, a warrant or entitlement, something short of the thing itself. 3 Nephi 9:17 removes the word: 'to them have I given to become the Sons of God.' What John holds at one remove the Book of Mormon grants outright, and the removal is precise enough to be a reading of John rather than a slip. The 1830's capitalized 'Sons of God' makes the same point typographically.

9:17.note: 'And as many as have received me, to them have I given to become the Sons of God; and even so will I to as many as shall believe on my name.' John 1:12 in the first person, following John 1:11 in 9:16 as John's own order requires, with the two King James singletons intact and 'power' dropped. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold — the longest continuous run is six words — and a quotation on any other reckoning.

9:18.text: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.

provenance.other: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:6 and 22:13, and “the beginning and the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, the same two. Revelation 1:8 is excluded by a single syllable: it reads 'the beginning and the ending'. “Alpha and Omega” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all in Revelation.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 1:8, which is the best-known of the four and the one a reader is likeliest to name — but its wording is not the Book of Mormon's.
provenance.significance: Ten continuous words, and the choice among Revelation's four self-identifications is settled by one word the Book of Mormon does not have. That matters beyond bookkeeping: Revelation 1:8 is spoken 'saith the Lord' by a voice describing itself in the third person to a seer, while 21:6 and 22:13 are spoken by Christ in his own person at the end of the book, one of them ('It is done') immediately after the new heaven and the new earth. 3 Nephi 9 speaks after a destruction that has remade the face of a land, and it takes the formula from the two places in Revelation where a world has just ended.

9:18.note: 'I am the light and the life of the world. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.' Ten words of Revelation continuously and exactly, in a first-person divine speech, as in the source. This is the strongest single verbal contact in the chapter and one of the cleanest anywhere in 3 Nephi; the only thing standing between it and Skousen's threshold is that his count needs sixteen.

9:18.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

provenance.other: “the light of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 5:14, John 8:12 and John 9:5 — of which Matthew's is addressed to the disciples and only John's two are self-predications. “the life of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:51. The Book of Mormon's 'the light and the life of the world' fuses two Johannine titles that the Gospel never joins.
provenance.significance: The compound is not in the Bible, and recovering its halves shows why it belongs here rather than anywhere else. John 8:12 promises that whoever follows the light of the world 'shall not walk in darkness' — and this speech is delivered into three days of a darkness so thick it could not be lighted (3 Nephi 8:20-23). John 6:51 makes Christ the life of the world by the giving of his flesh, which is the death this chapter has just described the sun going out over. The chapter fuses the two titles at precisely the moment when both are literally at issue: the light speaks in the dark, and the life speaks from the far side of its own death.

9:18.note: 'I am the light and the life of the world.' Neither half is a quotation and the compound is the Book of Mormon's own, but both halves are Johannine self-predications and one of them is a King James singleton. Graded high on the strength of the setting rather than the run length: a formula joining light and life to the world, spoken out of a three-day darkness by one who has just died, is not reaching past John for its vocabulary.

9:19.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James Bible has 'shed blood' and 'bloodshed' constantly; the nominalized 'shedding of blood' it uses once, in the verse that makes it the condition of remission.
provenance.significance: This is the sharpest metalepsis in the chapter. The single King James verse containing the phrase 3 Nephi 9:19 abolishes is the verse that says the thing being abolished is indispensable: 'without shedding of blood is no remission.' The abolition is therefore not a repudiation of Hebrews but its conclusion — the sacrifices end because the one shedding of blood that Hebrews 9 is arguing toward has now happened, three days earlier, and the chapter has just described the sky going dark over it. Hebrews 10:9 supplies the mechanism in the same first person the Book of Mormon uses: 'He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second.' 3 Nephi 9:19-20 takes away the first in verse 19 and establishes the second in verse 20.

9:19.note: 'And ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood; yea, your sacrifices and your burnt offerings shall be done away.' Three words, and they are a King James singleton belonging to the one New Testament argument this sentence is executing. The Old Testament has plenty of verses rejecting sacrifice — Psalm 51:16, Isaiah 1:11, Jeremiah 6:20, Amos 5:22 — but every one of them rejects sacrifice as insincere, and none of them abolishes it; Hebrews 9-10 is the only place in the Bible where the whole system is ended by a single blood-shedding, which is what 3 Nephi 9:19 announces.

9:20.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.other: “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. Psalm 34:18 is therefore the only verse in the King James Bible containing both, and it contains them in the Book of Mormon's order. Psalm 51:17, which readers reflexively name here, has the nouns crossed: 'a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart'.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 51:17, on the strength of its subject — it is the Bible's classic statement that God prefers a contrite heart to sacrifice, which is the argument 9:19-20 is making. But its wording is not this wording; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Getting the psalm right changes what the verse promises. Psalm 51 offers the broken heart as what God will not despise — a negative, a plea from a penitent that his offering not be rejected. Psalm 34:18 offers it as the condition on which 'the LORD is nigh' and 'saveth', which is exactly what 3 Nephi 9:20 goes on to give: whoever brings it is baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost. The Book of Mormon's sacrifice is not accepted grudgingly in place of a bullock; it is the thing that brings God near, and that is Psalm 34's claim and not Psalm 51's.

9:20.note: 'Ye shall offer for a sacrifice unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' Two rare King James collocations that meet in one verse and in this order, and a distribution that decides between the two psalms a reader would propose. The catalogue has taken the same pair to Psalm 34:18 at 2 Nephi 2:7, 2 Nephi 4:32 and Jacob 2:10; this is its first appearance in 3 Nephi and its first appearance in a divine first-person speech, where the sacrificial framing of 9:19 makes the Psalm 51 alternative genuinely tempting and the wording still refuses it.

9:20.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.route: Matthew 3:11 / Luke 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 — the Baptist's saying in its two fuller forms; Mark 1:8 and John 1:33 omit the fire. Both KJV verses put the Holy Ghost first and the fire second, and 3 Nephi 9:20 reverses them, twice in one verse: 'baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost'.
provenance.significance: The inversion is consistent and it is doing work. In the Gospels the fire is the second, ominous term — the next verse in both Matthew and Luke burns the chaff 'with unquenchable fire', so the Baptist's fire is judgement appended to blessing. 3 Nephi 9:20 puts the fire first, in a chapter that has just burned four cities with fire and buried the rest, and thereby claims the same element for mercy. The Lamanites who 'were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not' are the proof offered: fire that arrives unnoticed and saves, in a chapter where fire has been arriving very noticeably and destroying.

9:20.note: 'Him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost, even as the Lamanites … were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not.' The Baptist's promise, with the two elements transposed. The transposition is not an error to be explained away — it is repeated within the verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's standing order for the phrase — but it does mean the run is not continuous with either Gospel, which is why this is an allusion rather than a quotation despite the vocabulary being complete.

9:21.text: And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.

provenance.other: “to save the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:47. The nearest competitor is 1 Timothy 1:15, where “the world to save” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners' — which supplies the Book of Mormon's 'come unto the world' but not its object.
provenance.significance: John 12:47 disclaims judgement, and this chapter has just executed one. The voice that has spent eighteen verses itemizing the cities it burned, sank and buried says, in the nineteenth, that it came not to judge but to save the world — using the one King James phrase for it, and using it eight verses after quoting John 12:40 at 9:13. The chapter is working in a single stretch of John's twelfth chapter, and the part of it it takes is the part that denies doing what the chapter has done.

9:21.note: 'Behold, I have come unto the world to bring redemption unto the world, to save the world from sin.' A King James singleton, tripled: 'the world' three times in one sentence where John has it twice. The link is moderate because the sentence is a summary formula the Book of Mormon could reach from several New Testament places at once, and because 'come unto the world' is 1 Timothy's construction rather than John's.
9:21.whyNot: 'To save the world' is short and the doctrine is the New Testament's common property; a reader who takes 1 Timothy 1:15 as the source, or no single source at all, is not being unreasonable.

9:22.text: But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: “of such is the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16; “as a little child” occurs in exactly two, Mark 10:15 and Luke 18:17. Matthew 19:14 is excluded by one word — it reads 'kingdom of heaven'. Mark and Luke cannot be separated on wording here, and the Book of Mormon has both halves of the pericope, the saying at verse 14 and the condition at verse 15.
provenance.significance: The chapter began by drowning a city in the depths of the sea and ends by receiving whoever comes as a little child. Those are the two ends of Mark's own material: the millstone and the deep for whoever offends a little one, and the kingdom for whoever becomes one. Recovering the source puts the destruction and the invitation in one frame rather than two, and answers the question the chapter otherwise leaves open — on what terms the survivors of a divine destruction are supposed to approach the God who caused it. On a child's terms, which is Mark's answer and not the chapter's own invention.

9:22.note: 'Whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive; for of such is the kingdom of God.' Eight continuous words of Mark 10:14 with the following verse's 'as a little child' folded in ahead of them. 'Kingdom of God' rather than Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven' rules out Matthew; nothing rules out Luke 18:16-17, which is identical in the shared span, and Mark is named as the source only because the Book of Mormon has the whole two-verse unit that Mark and Luke both carry. Below Skousen's threshold and a quotation on the evidence.

9:22.text: Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.

provenance.other: “lay down my life” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37, of which Peter speaks the third. “take it again” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:17 and 10:18. Only John 10:17 has both, and it is the only verse in the Bible where laying down a life and taking it again stand in one clause.
provenance.significance: John 10:17-18 is the good-shepherd claim that no man takes the life from him — that the laying down is voluntary and the taking again is a power he holds. 3 Nephi 9:22 puts that claim in the perfect tense: 'I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again.' John's Jesus says it prospectively to opponents who are about to stone him; here it is said retrospectively, three days after the fact, to survivors who felt the earth shake when it happened. The tense is the whole distance the Book of Mormon has travelled from its source, and it is the only word it changes.

9:22.note: 'For such I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again.' John 10:17's two clauses in John's order, moved from the future to the perfect and given 'up' — which John does not have, and which the resurrection makes natural. The verbs are rare enough to be decisive: nowhere else in the King James Bible does anyone speak of taking a laid-down life again.

9:22.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.other: “and be ye saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the ends of the earth” occurs in exactly twenty-eight, but Isaiah 45:22 is the only one in which God addresses them directly in the imperative and offers them salvation. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'come' for Isaiah's 'look', which is Matthew 11:28's verb — 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 45:22's second half is the reason the summons is worth recovering: 'for I am God, and there is none else.' It is the Old Testament's most compressed monotheistic self-declaration, and the invitation is grounded in it — look to me because there is nobody else to look to. 3 Nephi 9 opens with a voice identifying itself ('Behold I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God', 9:15) and closes by issuing Isaiah's summons to the ends of the earth in the first person. The unstated half of the source supplies the warrant the chapter never states: the speaker can call the ends of the earth to himself because he is the one Isaiah 45 says there is none else beside.

9:22.note: 'Therefore repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.' A King James singleton and the addressees, in Isaiah's order, with one verb changed. The change is not arbitrary: 'look' becomes 'come', which is the verb of Matthew 11:28 and of this chapter's own repeated 'whosoever will come, him will I receive' (9:14) and 'cometh unto me' (9:20, 9:22). Isaiah supplies the sentence; the Gospels supply the verb that makes the sentence about approach rather than sight.
